purpose: Canonical cultural layer for the 24 archipelago civilizations. This sits below regional architecture and above individual island flavor. Regions influence one another, but borrowed ideas must be translated through local climate, materials, craft traditions, institutions and history rather than copied literally.
global_rules: No civilization is a one-to-one copy of a real-world culture. Real-world logic may inspire development patterns, but each culture must remain internally derived from the archipelago's own geography and history.
Rural vernacular changes slowest and should look most local. Ports, capitals, guild districts and elite buildings may show stronger outside influence.
A borrowed structural idea must be rebuilt using local materials and local construction logic before it becomes culturally accepted.
Neighboring regions should share transitional details at borders and trade ports, but their core settlement silhouettes must remain distinguishable.
Signature structures are rare. Ordinary houses, workshops, barns, shrines, roads and docks should carry most of the cultural identity.
Festivals, food, burial practice, public space, transport and naming should reinforce architecture rather than act as disconnected lore.
Cultures evolve. Older districts may preserve earlier forms while newer districts show imported techniques or post-treaty standards.
The Grand Exchange and Transit Isles are the strongest cultural mixing zones; the Great Cold North and Shrouded Isles are among the least externally transformed.

The Great Cold North.naming_convention: Short, weighty compound names tied to weather, landforms, animals and kin halls; settlements often end in Hall, Hold, Vale or Watch.
The Great Cold North.emblem: A white antler beneath a dark northern star.
The Great Cold North.materials_and_palette: Dark spruce, pale stone, packed snow, iron fittings, muted wool, weathered copper used sparingly.
The Great Cold North.clothing: Heavy layered wool, fur-lined cloaks, broad belts, simple metal clasps and practical winter hoods; status appears in weaving and clasp-work rather than bright color.
The Great Cold North.food: Smoked fish, roasted root crops, preserved meat, dark bread, stews and strong warming brews.
The Great Cold North.festival: First Fire — the first major winter gathering, when scattered households return to communal halls and relight shared hearths.
The Great Cold North.faith_and_ritual: Ancestor and landscape reverence expressed through cairns, standing stones, hall posts and seasonal hearth rites rather than a centralized priesthood.
The Great Cold North.burial: Stone cairns, ridge graves and memorial posts placed where wind and sky remain visible.
The Great Cold North.public_space: The communal hall is the civic center; open plazas are rare because gathering happens indoors.
The Great Cold North.transport_style: Sled roads, marked winter trails, beacon cairns and protected landing coves.
The Great Cold North.vessel_style: Deep-sided, sturdy northern boats with high bows and enclosed cargo sections.
The Great Cold North.everyday_feel: Sparse, quiet and communal. A settlement feels small against the landscape, but every inhabited structure feels durable and socially important.
The Great Cold North.distinctiveness_rule: Even prestigious imported ideas must remain broad, low and winter-protective rather than becoming elegant or vertical.

Frost Marches.naming_convention: Frontier names based on rivers, crossings, woods and founders; common endings include Ford, Crossing, March, Gate and Hearth.
Frost Marches.emblem: A covered bridge beneath three falling snow marks.
Frost Marches.materials_and_palette: Spruce and fir timber, fieldstone, dark shingles, wool awnings, iron straps.
Frost Marches.clothing: Layered but lighter than the far north; quilted coats, work aprons, hooded capes and visible guild or town badges.
Frost Marches.food: Smoked meats, grain porridge, hardy vegetables, forest mushrooms, berry preserves and lighter ales.
Frost Marches.festival: Opening of the Roads — spring clearing of routes followed by markets, repairs and matchmaking fairs.
Frost Marches.faith_and_ritual: Roadside shrines and refuge chapels emphasize safe travel, hospitality and remembrance of those lost in winter.
Frost Marches.burial: Small fenced family plots or chapel yards close to settlements rather than isolated cairns.
Frost Marches.public_space: Covered market streets and bridge plazas; civic life gathers where travelers naturally pass.
Frost Marches.transport_style: Covered bridges, timber causeways, snow roads and compact caravan yards.
Frost Marches.vessel_style: Practical river and coastal cargo craft, less specialized than Shattered Ice Coast ships.
Frost Marches.everyday_feel: Busy frontier practicality: merchants, timber workers, farmers and travelers share compact protected streets.
Frost Marches.distinctiveness_rule: Imported forms are simplified, enclosed and made repairable by ordinary frontier builders.

Shattered Ice Coast.naming_convention: Sea- and storm-based names; harbors often reference wrecks, beacons, capes, chains, bergs and sheltered coves.
Shattered Ice Coast.emblem: A red beacon above a broken white wave.
Shattered Ice Coast.materials_and_palette: Salt-darkened timber, gray stone, salvaged hull planks, iron chains, limited bright beacon paint.
Shattered Ice Coast.clothing: Waterproof-looking layered coats, heavy gloves, high boots, knitted caps and colored rescue scarves used for visibility.
Shattered Ice Coast.food: Cold-water fish, smoked and salted foods, seaweed, hard bread, stews and hot dockside drinks.
Shattered Ice Coast.festival: Beacon Night — every navigation light is lit together to honor rescuers, sailors and those lost at sea.
Shattered Ice Coast.faith_and_ritual: Sea chapels, memorial bells and rescue oaths; religious practice is strongly tied to maritime duty.
Shattered Ice Coast.burial: Cliffside memorial stones and empty graves for those never recovered from the sea.
Shattered Ice Coast.public_space: Protected inner harbors, repair yards and guild halls function as social centers.
Shattered Ice Coast.transport_style: Beacon chains, ice-marked sea lanes, enclosed docks and rescue stations.
Shattered Ice Coast.vessel_style: Reinforced hulls, compact rigs, high bows and visible salvaged repairs treated as honorable scars.
Shattered Ice Coast.everyday_feel: Harsh but cooperative. The culture expects weather to win eventually, so maintenance and rescue are communal obligations.
Shattered Ice Coast.distinctiveness_rule: Nothing is decorative if it makes a structure more vulnerable to wind, ice or salt.

The Crownlands.naming_convention: Formal civic names tied to founders, laws, gates, plazas, saints, rulers and administrative functions; streets and districts are systematically named.
The Crownlands.emblem: A gold arch enclosing an iron crown.
The Crownlands.materials_and_palette: Dressed stone, polished andesite-like tones, dark roofs, restrained banners, ironwork and formal gardens.
The Crownlands.clothing: Structured coats, tailored tunics, civic colors, metal clasps and rank-specific sashes; uniforms are common in official roles.
The Crownlands.food: A cosmopolitan central cuisine combining Breadbasket grain, Hearthlands brewing, imported fish, meats and formal banquet traditions.
The Crownlands.festival: Concord Day — public ceremonies, markets, military displays and civic awards marking the legal union of the lowland towns.
The Crownlands.faith_and_ritual: Institutional temples, civic chapels and ceremonial processions; religion and government remain distinct but visibly intertwined in public ritual.
The Crownlands.burial: Ordered cemeteries, family crypts and memorial statuary; elite tombs emphasize lineage and public service.
The Crownlands.public_space: Formal squares, arcades, processional streets, gardens and civic halls deliberately planned as expressions of order.
The Crownlands.transport_style: Paved roads, milestone systems, formal bridges, guarded gates and regulated ports.
The Crownlands.vessel_style: State and merchant vessels with standardized hull plans, visible registry marks and disciplined dock organization.
The Crownlands.everyday_feel: Organized, legible and institutional. Even ordinary neighborhoods feel connected to systems of law, markets and public works.
The Crownlands.distinctiveness_rule: Foreign ideas are formalized, standardized and given civic hierarchy before entering mainstream use.

The High Kingdom.naming_convention: Elevated names tied to peaks, saints, dynasties, bridges, monasteries and noble houses; place names often sound ceremonial.
The High Kingdom.emblem: A silver tower rising between two mountain peaks.
The High Kingdom.materials_and_palette: Pale and dark stone contrasts, slate-like roofs, narrow banners, carved stone details, limited gilding on sacred or royal buildings.
The High Kingdom.clothing: Long layered garments, heavy cloaks, narrow decorative trim, house colors and carefully made boots suited to steep terrain.
The High Kingdom.food: Cheeses, preserved meats, mountain herbs, dense breads, orchard products from lower terraces and ceremonial wines or ales.
The High Kingdom.festival: Bridge Ascension — processions climb from valley settlements to high bridges and monasteries, celebrating unity across difficult terrain.
The High Kingdom.faith_and_ritual: Monastic traditions, bell towers, observatories and pilgrimage stairs; elevation itself carries spiritual meaning.
The High Kingdom.burial: Cliff crypts, monastery vaults and family tomb chambers carved into stable rock.
The High Kingdom.public_space: Terraced plazas, monumental stairs, bridge courts and monastery forecourts rather than broad flat squares.
The High Kingdom.transport_style: Switchback roads, stair streets, cliff bridges, lifts and guarded passes.
The High Kingdom.vessel_style: Limited maritime tradition; state barges and lake craft favor tall ceremonial profiles when used.
The High Kingdom.everyday_feel: Vertical, ceremonial and status-aware; ordinary daily movement constantly crosses stairs, terraces and bridges.
The High Kingdom.distinctiveness_rule: Practical masonry is elevated into symbolic and vertical form; prestige is expressed through height and difficult access.

The Hearthlands.naming_convention: Warm domestic names tied to lakes, mills, orchards, inns, bridges and founding families; many places retain old informal nicknames.
The Hearthlands.emblem: A copper kettle above three blue lake lines.
The Hearthlands.materials_and_palette: Warm timber, fieldstone, plaster, brick hearths, flower boxes, copper or dark iron accents.
The Hearthlands.clothing: Layered work clothes, aprons, knitted garments, colorful scarves and festival waistcoats; practical but intentionally welcoming.
The Hearthlands.food: The archipelago's richest comfort-food culture: breads, stews, cheeses, smoked meats, pastries, cider, beer and seasonal lake dishes.
The Hearthlands.festival: Long Table Week — villages set communal tables along streets and waterfronts, with each household contributing food and drink.
The Hearthlands.faith_and_ritual: Household shrines, bells, seasonal blessings and community feasts; formal clergy matters less than shared observance.
The Hearthlands.burial: Small garden cemeteries and family plots near villages, often planted with fruit trees or flowers.
The Hearthlands.public_space: Inn squares, covered bridges, brewery yards and waterfront greens designed around lingering rather than ceremony.
The Hearthlands.transport_style: Ferries, covered bridges, lake roads and frequent inns at route junctions.
The Hearthlands.vessel_style: Broad stable lake boats, ferries and cargo barges with covered passenger areas.
The Hearthlands.everyday_feel: Cozy, social and lived-in. Production, homes and gathering spaces overlap instead of being rigidly separated.
The Hearthlands.distinctiveness_rule: Imported ideas are reduced to human scale and made comfortable before they become culturally normal.

The Timberlands.naming_convention: Names refer to groves, mills, rivers, tree species, cuts, guilds and notable frames; professional titles often attach to place names.
The Timberlands.emblem: A dark green tree framed by a timber truss.
The Timberlands.materials_and_palette: Every wood family expressed structurally, stone only where needed, rope, iron brackets and restrained green guild marks.
The Timberlands.clothing: Durable workwear, leather aprons, tool belts, layered shirts and guild-marked caps or shoulder pieces.
The Timberlands.food: Forest mushrooms, game-style dishes, imported grain, smoked foods, berries and portable worker meals.
The Timberlands.festival: Raising Day — communities assemble a major timber frame together, followed by feasting beneath the unfinished structure.
The Timberlands.faith_and_ritual: Stewardship rites around old-growth groves, first-cut ceremonies and guild oaths concerning replanting and fire safety.
The Timberlands.burial: Wooded memorial groves with carved posts and stone footings rather than dense cemeteries.
The Timberlands.public_space: Guild yards, mill ponds, covered work streets and enormous frame halls that double as civic gathering spaces.
The Timberlands.transport_style: Log roads, river booms, timber bridges and forest rail or cart corridors.
The Timberlands.vessel_style: Strong practical timber cargo craft, barges and log-raft systems.
The Timberlands.everyday_feel: Craft-proud and visibly structural. People notice joints, spans, grain and repair quality the way other cultures notice ornament.
The Timberlands.distinctiveness_rule: Structure itself is decoration; imported ornament should never hide how a building stands.

The Breadbasket.naming_convention: Names tied to fields, canals, mills, locks, orchards and old farm estates; administrative water districts have numbered or functional names.
The Breadbasket.emblem: A gold sheaf crossed by a blue canal.
The Breadbasket.materials_and_palette: Plaster, timber, brick, fieldstone, pale farm walls, dark roofs and strong blue canal markers.
The Breadbasket.clothing: Practical farm clothing, broad hats, aprons, waterproof canal garments and seasonal festival embroidery.
The Breadbasket.food: Bread, grains, vegetables, preserves, dairy, fruit and simple high-volume market foods; much of the archipelago's staple cuisine starts here.
The Breadbasket.festival: Opening of the Locks — irrigation gates are ceremonially opened before planting season with markets and boat races.
The Breadbasket.faith_and_ritual: Seasonal blessings of water, seed and harvest; local water councils carry near-sacred civic legitimacy.
The Breadbasket.burial: Family plots along old field boundaries, village churchyards and tree-lined memorial lanes.
The Breadbasket.public_space: Mill squares, canal basins, produce markets and broad greens beside granaries.
The Breadbasket.transport_style: Canal barges, towpaths, farm roads, locks and mill bridges.
The Breadbasket.vessel_style: Flat-bottomed barges and low cargo boats optimized for canals and bulk food movement.
The Breadbasket.everyday_feel: Open, productive and seasonal; fields and waterworks dominate views more than buildings do.
The Breadbasket.distinctiveness_rule: Everything must remain subordinate to land and water management; prestige buildings still respect field geometry and canal access.

The Grand Exchange.naming_convention: Districts, quays and streets named after traded goods, guilds, foreign ports, founders and counting houses; names change more often than elsewhere.
The Grand Exchange.emblem: Four interlocking rings around a central scale.
The Grand Exchange.materials_and_palette: Deliberately mixed imported materials unified by repeated awnings, quay stone, signage and merchant heraldry.
The Grand Exchange.clothing: The most varied clothing in the world; merchant houses use recognizable colors, badges and coats while dock labor remains practical and mixed.
The Grand Exchange.food: A constantly changing fusion cuisine built from imported ingredients; street food, taverns and merchant dining halls are culturally important.
The Grand Exchange.festival: Open Quays — tariff suspensions, auctions, foreign delegations, night markets and public guild competitions.
The Grand Exchange.faith_and_ritual: Highly pluralistic; small foreign shrines coexist with merchant chapels, guild oaths and civic contracts treated almost ceremonially.
The Grand Exchange.burial: Dense urban cemeteries, family crypts and memorial halls funded by guilds or merchant houses.
The Grand Exchange.public_space: Covered markets, exchange courts, quays, auction squares and warehouse streets where commerce is itself public life.
The Grand Exchange.transport_style: Dense dock networks, cranes, freight alleys, ferries and standardized cargo handling.
The Grand Exchange.vessel_style: Every ship type appears, but local merchant vessels favor modular cargo handling and recognizable house markings.
The Grand Exchange.everyday_feel: Crowded, noisy, mixed and opportunistic; foreign architecture is common but always repurposed for trade density.
The Grand Exchange.distinctiveness_rule: Its identity comes from how many influences coexist under commercial rules, not from one material palette.

Engineer's Reach.naming_convention: Functional names, inventor names, yard numbers, line names and machine-related nicknames; official and worker names often differ.
Engineer's Reach.emblem: A redstone spark inside a gear-like square frame.
Engineer's Reach.materials_and_palette: Brick, stone, iron, copper, glass, exposed mechanisms and utility markings.
Engineer's Reach.clothing: Work coats, tool aprons, protective goggles/helmets in visual language, guild pins and high-visibility utility markings.
Engineer's Reach.food: Fast worker meals, canteens, imported Hearthlands comfort food and Grand Exchange street food.
Engineer's Reach.festival: Demonstration Week — workshops publicly unveil machines, bridges and transport prototypes, with awards for elegance and reliability.
Engineer's Reach.faith_and_ritual: Mostly secular guild culture; rituals focus on apprenticeship, first activation, memorial bells for industrial accidents and professional oaths.
Engineer's Reach.burial: Compact civic cemeteries and guild memorial walls engraved with professions and major works.
Engineer's Reach.public_space: Test yards, covered worker halls, demonstration plazas and rail concourses.
Engineer's Reach.transport_style: Rail, lifts, service tunnels, gantries and highly standardized loading routes.
Engineer's Reach.vessel_style: Experimental utility craft and transport prototypes rather than a traditional native ship style.
Engineer's Reach.everyday_feel: Active, technical and iterative; unfinished prototypes and maintenance access are normal parts of the streetscape.
Engineer's Reach.distinctiveness_rule: Any borrowed form is judged by serviceability, repeatability and access before aesthetics.

Artisan Coast.naming_convention: Names reference colors, workshops, masters, courts, flowers, glass, kilns and coastal landmarks.
Artisan Coast.emblem: A many-petaled glass rosette above a blue wave.
Artisan Coast.materials_and_palette: Glass, glazed terracotta, concrete-like blocks, pale plaster, tile, colorful awnings and decorative stone.
Artisan Coast.clothing: Layered artisan garments, patterned aprons, dyed fabrics, jewelry and visible craft-house motifs.
Artisan Coast.food: Colorful small dishes, baked goods, imported seafood, spiced market food and elaborate festival sweets.
Artisan Coast.festival: Night of a Hundred Lanterns — workshops illuminate streets with colored glass, banners and temporary installations.
Artisan Coast.faith_and_ritual: Patron shrines for crafts, guild blessing ceremonies and public dedication of major works rather than a single dominant institution.
Artisan Coast.burial: Decorative memorial courts, tiled markers and family niches integrated into garden cemeteries.
Artisan Coast.public_space: Workshop streets, shaded courtyards, arcades, gallery markets and seaside promenades.
Artisan Coast.transport_style: Pedestrian craft districts, coastal carts, compact docks and merchant ferries.
Artisan Coast.vessel_style: Elegant merchant and fishing boats with painted or glazed decorative details.
Artisan Coast.everyday_feel: Dense, expressive and social; making things happens visibly in the street rather than behind industrial walls.
Artisan Coast.distinctiveness_rule: Imported structure becomes a surface for craft expression, but decoration must still reveal the workshop function beneath it.

The Haunted Marches.naming_convention: Defensive and memorial names tied to walls, bells, wards, ruined estates, forests and famous stands.
The Haunted Marches.emblem: A black tower behind a white lantern.
The Haunted Marches.materials_and_palette: Dark timber, reused stone, iron bars, muted plaster, lantern-heavy streets and intentionally limited bright color.
The Haunted Marches.clothing: Heavy practical coats, leather protection, hooded capes, watch badges and mourning bands commonly worn as civic symbols.
The Haunted Marches.food: Preserved food, stews, mushrooms, smoked meats and imported Hearthlands staples; food culture values reliability over luxury.
The Haunted Marches.festival: Night Watch — citizens maintain lantern lines, ring ward bells and tell stories of failed settlements before a dawn communal meal.
The Haunted Marches.faith_and_ritual: Funerary chapels, warding customs, bell traditions and strong remembrance of the dead; ritual and defense overlap.
The Haunted Marches.burial: Walled cemeteries, ossuaries and fortified graveyards kept close enough to protect and remember.
The Haunted Marches.public_space: Protected inner yards, ward squares and gate courts rather than exposed plazas.
The Haunted Marches.transport_style: Patrolled roads, lantern routes, fortified bridges and watch stations.
The Haunted Marches.vessel_style: Few native ship traditions; practical guarded ferries and supply boats dominate.
The Haunted Marches.everyday_feel: Alert and communal, with doors, shutters, bells and sightlines constantly reminding the player that safety is built rather than assumed.
The Haunted Marches.distinctiveness_rule: Comfort exists, but every imported comfortable feature is hardened behind defensible thresholds.

The Blackfen.naming_convention: Names tied to channels, reeds, lanterns, trees, ferries, pools and local families; waterways often matter more than land parcels.
The Blackfen.emblem: A green lantern hanging above three reed stems.
The Blackfen.materials_and_palette: Mangrove and dark timber, mossy stone, reeds, rope, muted green/brown surfaces and warm lantern light.
The Blackfen.clothing: Light layered clothing, waterproof boots, broad hats, herb satchels, reed capes and bright route scarves for visibility in mist.
The Blackfen.food: Fish, mushrooms, herbs, frog-related visual motifs without literal exoticism, stews, pickled vegetables and medicinal teas.
The Blackfen.festival: Lantern Drift — families float lights along waterways to map safe channels and remember settlements lost to shifting water.
The Blackfen.faith_and_ritual: Marsh shrines, herbal rites, seasonal water blessings and ancestor lantern traditions.
The Blackfen.burial: Raised burial islands, tree-root memorials and lantern vigils rather than low ground graves.
The Blackfen.public_space: Market bridges, widened boardwalk nodes, ferry platforms and roofed communal decks.
The Blackfen.transport_style: Punts, ferries, pole boats, boardwalks and beacon poles; roads are culturally secondary.
The Blackfen.vessel_style: Shallow-draft boats with narrow hulls, roofed cargo sections and pole propulsion.
The Blackfen.everyday_feel: Fluid and intimate; neighborhoods are defined by channel access and boardwalk distance rather than street grids.
The Blackfen.distinctiveness_rule: Heavy imported architecture must be lightened, raised or broken into smaller pieces before it belongs in Blackfen.

Stone Highlands.naming_convention: Names tied to quarries, ridges, passes, bridges, stone types and guild founders; professional reputation strongly shapes place names.
Stone Highlands.emblem: A gray arch carrying a white mountain block.
Stone Highlands.materials_and_palette: Local stone families, heavy timber only for roofs and cranes, iron fittings, muted earth tones and quarry dust.
Stone Highlands.clothing: Durable layered work clothes, heavy boots, leather aprons, guild belts and dust-colored cloaks.
Stone Highlands.food: Dense breads, stews, cheeses, preserved meats and imported produce; communal quarry meals are culturally important.
Stone Highlands.festival: Setting of the Keystone — master masons build a public arch or bridge segment while apprentices compete in stonework.
Stone Highlands.faith_and_ritual: Guild oaths, hill shrines and memorial stones; craft lineage often matters as much as formal religion.
Stone Highlands.burial: Rock-cut family chambers, stone cairns and guild memorial walls.
Stone Highlands.public_space: Terraced squares, quarry amphitheaters, bridge yards and retaining-wall streets.
Stone Highlands.transport_style: Inclined haul roads, stone bridges, cliff roads, heavy freight routes and railheads.
Stone Highlands.vessel_style: Heavy cargo barges and stone freighters built elsewhere but modified for block handling.
Stone Highlands.everyday_feel: Solid, practical and craft-conscious; even modest buildings feel intentionally anchored into terrain.
Stone Highlands.distinctiveness_rule: The culture distrusts unnecessary height and ornament unless structure justifies it.

Red Clay Basin.naming_convention: Names tied to colors, cisterns, kilns, mesas, courtyards, wells and pottery guilds.
Red Clay Basin.emblem: A red vessel beneath a blue water line.
Red Clay Basin.materials_and_palette: Terracotta, brick, mud, packed earth, glazed tile, pale plaster and strong shadow from deep arcades.
Red Clay Basin.clothing: Light robes/tunics in visual language, head coverings, patterned belts, work aprons and bright glazed jewelry accents.
Red Clay Basin.food: Flat breads, roasted vegetables, legumes, preserved fruit, spiced stews and foods designed around communal shaded courtyards.
Red Clay Basin.festival: Firing Week — kilns across the basin are lit in sequence, with markets for new glazes and public repair of cisterns.
Red Clay Basin.faith_and_ritual: Water courts and household ancestor niches; stewardship of wells and cisterns carries moral as well as practical importance.
Red Clay Basin.burial: Rock-cut tombs, courtyard family crypts and ceramic memorial markers.
Red Clay Basin.public_space: Shaded bazaars, cistern plazas, arcades and interior courtyards rather than exposed open squares.
Red Clay Basin.transport_style: Terraced roads, caravan-style cargo courts, aqueduct paths and sheltered market streets.
Red Clay Basin.vessel_style: Trade barges and coastal cargo craft usually built by partners, distinguished locally through painted or glazed cargo containers.
Red Clay Basin.everyday_feel: Sun-conscious, craft-rich and courtyard-centered; public and private life transitions through shade rather than walls alone.
Red Clay Basin.distinctiveness_rule: Imported forms must first solve heat, shade or water before they are permitted to become decorative.

The Sunken Coast.naming_convention: Names tied to tides, bells, drowned landmarks, inlets, fish grounds and sea walls; old pre-flood place names remain common.
The Sunken Coast.emblem: A half-submerged bell inside a blue ring.
The Sunken Coast.materials_and_palette: Weathered timber, pale stone, seawall masonry, rope, kelp greens, faded blues and visible flood marks.
The Sunken Coast.clothing: Rolled trousers, waterproof capes, fisher knits, broad belts, diving/salvage gear in visual language and family boat colors.
The Sunken Coast.food: Fish, shellfish-like visual inspiration using Minecraft foods, kelp, smoked foods, grain imports and strong dockside soups.
The Sunken Coast.festival: Low Water Day — communities inspect old ruins, repair sea defenses and hold markets on ground usually covered by tide.
The Sunken Coast.faith_and_ritual: Storm chapels, drowned bells, sea-wall blessings and memorial processions for lost settlements.
The Sunken Coast.burial: Raised cemeteries and memorial towers; some old graveyards remain visible only at low water.
The Sunken Coast.public_space: Tidal markets, sea gates, piers and elevated council platforms.
The Sunken Coast.transport_style: Boats, causeways, tide gates, channel markers and raised footways.
The Sunken Coast.vessel_style: Broad shallow fishing craft, salvage boats and practical tide-compatible ferries.
The Sunken Coast.everyday_feel: Adaptive and layered; old ruins remain part of daily life and every settlement visibly negotiates with the water.
borrowed_from: Sapphire Coast seawalls and marine stonework
The Sunken Coast.distinctiveness_rule: Buildings should reveal historical water levels and adaptation rather than pretending the shoreline is permanent.

The Crystal Deep.naming_convention: Technical, acoustic and geometric names tied to chambers, resonances, shafts, vaults, geodes and numbered surveys.
The Crystal Deep.emblem: A violet crystal suspended inside a white geometric frame.
The Crystal Deep.materials_and_palette: Stone, deepslate-like blocks, amethyst, dark timber accents, copper mechanisms and carefully controlled low lighting.
The Crystal Deep.clothing: Close-fitting layered work clothes, harnesses, lamps, quiet footwear and color-coded research sashes or insignia.
The Crystal Deep.food: Imported surface staples supplemented by cave-grown berries, mushrooms and compact preserved foods.
The Crystal Deep.festival: Resonance Night — machinery pauses and communities gather in major chambers to hear natural echoes, bells and crystal tones.
The Crystal Deep.faith_and_ritual: A spectrum from scientific reverence to monastic contemplation; silence, geometry, sound and ancient ruins carry ritual weight.
The Crystal Deep.burial: Sealed wall niches, crystal memorial chambers and names recorded in archive halls rather than large surface-style cemeteries.
The Crystal Deep.public_space: Bridge junctions, cavern halls, lift stations and reflection pools; horizontal plazas are rare.
The Crystal Deep.transport_style: Lifts, suspended bridges, rail, vertical shafts and carefully marked quiet zones.
The Crystal Deep.vessel_style: No major native maritime tradition; expedition barges and underground freight carts dominate transport culture.
The Crystal Deep.everyday_feel: Quiet, technical and uncanny. Light, sound and vertical distance matter more than weather.
The Crystal Deep.distinctiveness_rule: Surface architecture must be carved, suspended or geometrically abstracted before it feels native underground.

The Volcano.naming_convention: Names reference calderas, forges, flows, vents, cooling courts and famous smithing houses.
The Volcano.emblem: A black mountain split by a gold-orange forge line.
The Volcano.materials_and_palette: Basalt, blackstone-like masonry, dark brick, iron, copper, controlled lava glow and pale cooling stone.
The Volcano.clothing: Heavy work aprons, heat-protective visual layers, short practical cloaks, gloves and metal guild marks.
The Volcano.food: Imported grains and produce, roasted foods, dense stews and communal shift meals prepared in heat-safe quarters.
The Volcano.festival: First Pour — annual ceremonial casting in the great forge, followed by night markets around safely channeled lava.
The Volcano.faith_and_ritual: Forge blessings, memorials for workers lost to heat and strong professional rites; the caldera is respected as dangerous rather than worshipped simply.
The Volcano.burial: Stone vaults in cooled ground, engraved forge markers and memorial walls in worker courtyards.
The Volcano.public_space: Cooling courts, forge plazas, covered worker halls and heat-buffered arcades.
The Volcano.transport_style: Causeways, protected lava crossings, heavy freight roads and geothermal industrial ports.
The Volcano.vessel_style: Heavy cargo craft with stone-protected loading quays; most hulls are imported or built by partners.
The Volcano.everyday_feel: Monumental, hot and disciplined; safety boundaries are culturally visible everywhere.
The Volcano.distinctiveness_rule: Even civic beauty must respect heat separation, cooling space and massive thermal structure.

Pirate Island.naming_convention: Nicknames, ship names, taverns, captains, accidents and jokes become official place names over time; maps often disagree.
Pirate Island.emblem: A patched sail over a broken crown.
Pirate Island.materials_and_palette: Salvaged ship timber, imported stone, mismatched roofs, rope, chains, painted signs and visibly reused architectural fragments.
Pirate Island.clothing: Highly mixed; practical sailor clothing, captured finery, foreign coats, belts, scarves and personal symbols matter more than uniform identity.
Pirate Island.food: Everything that can be traded, stolen or preserved; tavern food, imported spices, fish and strong drink dominate social life.
Pirate Island.festival: Freeport Founding — ship races, auctions, debt forgiveness rituals, tavern competitions and theatrical retellings of the freeport's origins.
Pirate Island.faith_and_ritual: Pluralistic shipboard shrines, luck customs, memorial walls and captain traditions; formal institutions are distrusted.
Pirate Island.burial: Sea memorials, cliff graves, shipyard markers and tavern plaques for famous crews.
Pirate Island.public_space: Tavern alleys, auction docks, rope bridges, shipyards and improvised squares where buildings happen to leave room.
Pirate Island.transport_style: Dense docks, hidden coves, rope paths, sea caves and informal ferries.
Pirate Island.vessel_style: Every style appears, but ships are heavily modified, patched and personalized rather than standardized.
Pirate Island.everyday_feel: Chaotic but functional. Rules exist, but they are social and negotiated rather than visually imposed by planning.
borrowed_from: Every maritime culture, especially Timberlands, Grand Exchange and Shattered Ice Coast
Pirate Island.distinctiveness_rule: Nothing should look designed all at once; the city must appear accumulated, captured, repaired and expanded over generations.

The Ember Coast.naming_convention: Names tied to portals, bastions, ash, courts, chains, furnaces and expedition companies; districts retain names from failed early expeditions.
The Ember Coast.emblem: A dark portal frame crossed by a bright ember line.
The Ember Coast.materials_and_palette: Blackstone/basalt, Nether brick, dark metal, crimson/warped vegetation accents, controlled lava and highly visible safety markings.
The Ember Coast.clothing: Protective-looking layered workwear, masks/hoods in visual language, district insignia and color-coded expedition gear.
The Ember Coast.food: Surface imports combined with Nether-grown ingredients where practical; preserved foods and secure communal mess halls dominate.
The Ember Coast.festival: Safe Return — expedition gates open ceremonially and successful crews add plaques to the First Safe Court.
The Ember Coast.faith_and_ritual: Portal oaths, memorial walls and strong safety rituals; superstition and engineering coexist because failures are historically costly.
The Ember Coast.burial: Surface-facing memorial courts, sealed vaults and expedition-name walls; bodies lost beyond portals may receive empty tombs.
The Ember Coast.public_space: Protected portal courts, fortified markets, furnace streets and compartmentalized district plazas.
The Ember Coast.transport_style: Guarded causeways, portal checkpoints, freight courts and highly controlled route signage.
The Ember Coast.vessel_style: Coastal heavy cargo craft; the civilization's distinctive transport culture is portal-based rather than maritime.
The Ember Coast.everyday_feel: Fortified, procedural and intense; crossing between districts feels like moving through controlled risk zones.
The Ember Coast.distinctiveness_rule: Foreign ideas are compartmentalized and hardened; convenience never overrides containment.

The Sapphire Coast.naming_convention: Names reference reefs, currents, gates, colors, marine creatures, towers and old navigator families.
The Sapphire Coast.emblem: A turquoise arch rising from a white wave.
The Sapphire Coast.materials_and_palette: Pale stone, prismarine, glass, coral accents, light wood, blue-green roofs and bright sunlit plazas.
The Sapphire Coast.clothing: Light coastal garments, sailor capes, blue-green sashes, pearl/prismarine-like jewelry motifs and formal navigator uniforms.
The Sapphire Coast.food: Fish, sea greens, tropical imports, citrus-like visual cues from available Minecraft foods and refined coastal market dishes.
The Sapphire Coast.festival: Opening of the Sea Gate — ceremonial fleet passage, reef lanterns, swimming/diving exhibitions and navigator honors.
The Sapphire Coast.faith_and_ritual: Sea-gate shrines, guardian symbolism, reef stewardship rites and formal remembrance of navigators.
The Sapphire Coast.burial: Sea-facing mausoleums, reef memorial gardens and tower crypts for notable navigators.
The Sapphire Coast.public_space: Water plazas, arcaded quays, sea stairs, reef gardens and monumental gates visible from both land and water.
The Sapphire Coast.transport_style: Canal-like sea streets, ferries, formal quays and lighthouse chains.
The Sapphire Coast.vessel_style: Elegant blue-water vessels with pale hull details, standardized navigational markings and disciplined crews.
The Sapphire Coast.everyday_feel: Bright, maritime and formal without being militarized; water is treated as civic space rather than boundary.
The Sapphire Coast.distinctiveness_rule: Imported waterfront ideas are regularized into symmetrical, ceremonial marine architecture.

The Isles of Plenty.naming_convention: Names tied to animals, orchards, flowers, coves, breezes, groves and founding families; names are often descriptive and affectionate.
The Isles of Plenty.emblem: A green leaf encircling a golden animal silhouette.
The Isles of Plenty.materials_and_palette: Light timber, bamboo, pale stone bases, bright textiles, lush planting and open shade structures.
The Isles of Plenty.clothing: Loose light garments, broad hats, bright woven belts, sandals/boots depending on work and floral or animal household motifs.
The Isles of Plenty.food: Fruit, honey, melons, animal products, breads, tropical crops and abundant fresh market food.
The Isles of Plenty.festival: Festival of Plenty — open-air markets, animal shows, bee gardens, communal cooking and decorated waterfronts.
The Isles of Plenty.faith_and_ritual: Household and grove shrines emphasizing fertility, stewardship, rain and animal care rather than centralized religion.
The Isles of Plenty.burial: Garden burial grounds, orchard memorials and small family shrines integrated into cultivated landscapes.
The Isles of Plenty.public_space: Open pavilions, shaded markets, waterfront greens and animal-friendly courtyards.
The Isles of Plenty.transport_style: Coastal boats, farm paths, light bridges and shaded roadways.
The Isles of Plenty.vessel_style: Light colorful coastal craft optimized for produce, animals and short regional routes.
The Isles of Plenty.everyday_feel: Open, lush and relaxed; settlements feel porous, with animals, gardens and workspaces flowing through civic life.
The Isles of Plenty.distinctiveness_rule: Heavy imported forms are opened, shaded and surrounded by planting until they feel climate-appropriate.

The Transit Isles.naming_convention: Functional route names, station numbers, lighthouse names, famous pilots and old ferry crossings; unofficial traveler names often become permanent.
The Transit Isles.emblem: Four arrows meeting at a single white marker.
The Transit Isles.materials_and_palette: Mixed regional materials unified by route markings, standardized signs, platform geometry and repeated signal elements.
The Transit Isles.clothing: Practical travel clothing, station uniforms, pilot coats, messenger bags, route badges and standardized staff colors.
The Transit Isles.food: Traveler food from every region: portable meals, inns, market halls and station canteens rather than one native cuisine.
The Transit Isles.festival: Accords Week — free or ceremonial travel on major routes, station competitions, pilot honors and public route-map updates.
The Transit Isles.faith_and_ritual: Pluralistic traveler shrines, departure bells, memorial markers for lost routes and strong professional codes among pilots and station keepers.
The Transit Isles.burial: Small neutral cemeteries and memorial walls listing origins as well as service in the Transit network.
The Transit Isles.public_space: Terminals, concourses, inns, platforms and waiting halls; movement spaces are the culture's civic spaces.
The Transit Isles.transport_style: Rail, ferry, rockets, lighthouses, bridgeheads, freight transfer and standardized emergency routes.
The Transit Isles.vessel_style: Standardized ferries, pilot boats and service craft designed for interoperability with many ports.
The Transit Isles.everyday_feel: Constant motion, multilingual visual culture and strong wayfinding; strangers are normal, confusion is culturally unacceptable.
The Transit Isles.distinctiveness_rule: Local identity comes from standardizing movement across foreign styles, never from erasing those styles completely.

The Shrouded Isles.naming_convention: Sparse, abstract and often deliberately indirect names tied to veils, stars, intervals, silence, observations and expedition codes.
The Shrouded Isles.emblem: A black eye-like oval beneath a broken violet star.
The Shrouded Isles.materials_and_palette: Obsidian, purpur-like materials, dark stone, pale accents, chorus vegetation and selectively reused mainland materials.
The Shrouded Isles.clothing: Layered travel garments adapted from many origins, face-covering hoods in visual language, muted fabrics and small violet or black expedition marks.
The Shrouded Isles.food: Mostly imported ordinary foods supplemented by chorus-derived local resources; meals remain culturally tied to expedition ration traditions.
The Shrouded Isles.festival: The Unveiling — a rare open gathering when normally closed observatories and archives display discoveries to trusted visitors.
The Shrouded Isles.faith_and_ritual: Highly diverse private beliefs, but common ritual focuses on observation, silence, safe return and the psychological boundary between home and the End.
The Shrouded Isles.burial: Memorial chambers, name walls and empty markers for people who vanished beyond known routes; locations are intentionally secluded.
The Shrouded Isles.public_space: Sparse observatory courts, hidden meeting rooms and isolated plazas connected by long quiet paths.
The Shrouded Isles.transport_style: Restricted portal routes, concealed docks, long wilderness approaches and controlled expedition staging.
The Shrouded Isles.vessel_style: No dominant native ship style; expedition craft are adapted from Transit and home-region designs, then stripped down for secrecy and endurance.
The Shrouded Isles.everyday_feel: Quiet, distant and slightly unfamiliar even when structures use recognizable mainland forms.
The Shrouded Isles.distinctiveness_rule: Borrowed forms should remain recognizable at first glance but have altered proportions, access logic or spacing that makes them subtly alien.
